claim: On SWE-PRBench, no frontier model detects more than 31% of human-flagged issues from a diff alone (mean ~26% across 8 models), leaving a 20-40 percentage-point gap to human reviewers.
quote: no model detects more than 31% of human-flagged issues on the diff-only configuration ... the mean detection rate across all 8 models on config_A is approximately 26% ... the gap to human performance is approximately 20-40 percentage points

claim: On CR-Bench, a single-shot GPT-5.2 code-review agent scored 3.56% precision, 27.01% recall and 6.30% F1; a Reflexion variant raised recall to 32.76% but precision only to 5.10% (F1 8.83%), collapsing signal-to-noise from 5.11 to 1.95.
quote: Single-shot Agent (GPT-5.2): Recall: 27.01% Precision: 3.56% F1 Score: 6.30% Signal-to-Noise Ratio: 5.11 ... Reflexion Agent (GPT-5.2): Recall: 32.76% Precision: 5.10% F1 Score: 8.83% Signal-to-Noise Ratio: 1.95

claim: An empirical study of 19,450 AIDev PRs found 12 of 13 code-review agents have average signal ratios below 60%, with 60.2% of closed CRA-only PRs falling in the 0-30% signal range, indicating substantial review noise.
quote: 60.2% of closed CRA-only PRs fall into the 0-30% signal range ... 12 of 13 CRAs exhibit average signal ratios below 60%, indicating substantial noise in automated review feedback

claim: A Martian benchmark over 200,000 real PRs (Jan-Feb 2026) found the top-disclosed tool reached only 51.7% F1 (52.2% precision, 51.1% recall) while the rest of 17 tools sat near one-in-four precision.
quote: F1 Score: 51.7% Precision: 52.2% Recall: 51.1% ... the rest of the category is closer to one in four

claim: Industry false-positive rates for even the best AI code review systems sit in the 5-15% range, driven by single-line context, pattern-not-certainty inference, and missing domain knowledge.
quote: Industry benchmarks suggest that even the best AI-driven code review systems today typically achieve false-positive rates in the 5-15% range ... They may flag edge cases, misunderstand domain-specific logic, or lack context about why certain code patterns were chosen

claim: A 28-PR audit of CodeRabbit found 15% of its comments were useless/noise and 21% were nitpicking, with each inline comment firing a separate GitHub notification so teammates began auto-dismissing it within ~1.5 weeks.
quote: An audit of 28 PRs found 15% of CodeRabbit's comments were Useless/Noise and 21% were Nitpicking ... after about a week and a half, teammates were auto-dismissing CodeRabbit the way they auto-dismiss Dependabot alerts

claim: A practitioner reports AI reviewers find new things to comment on after every change, producing an 'endless loop' of refinement, and observed an AI reviewing its own suggestion then advising reverting to the original code.
quote: on every change, the AI keeps finding new things to comment on. You can end up in a sort of 'endless loop' of refinement if you're not careful

claim: CVE-2025-53773 allowed RCE via prompt injection in GitHub Copilot by injecting content that makes the agent write 'chat.tools.autoApprove': true into .vscode/settings.json, disabling all user confirmations.
quote: The prompt injection first adds the line 'chat.tools.autoApprove': true, to the ~/.vscode/settings.json file.

claim: CodeRabbit states it does not retain source code after review (except when caching is enabled), never uses code for training, and is SOC 2 Type II certified and GDPR compliant.
quote: CodeRabbit does not retain your source code after a review completes, except when review caching is enabled... encrypted, used only to accelerate reviews, never used for training, and expires automatically... CodeRabbit is SOC Type II certified and GDPR compliant

claim: The 'Comment and Control' attack (disclosed April 2026, Aonan Guan et al.) used HTML-comment-hidden instructions in PR titles/issue comments to make Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and GitHub Copilot Agent leak credentials including GITHUB_TOKEN, GITHUB_COPILOT_API_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and GEMINI_API_KEY.
quote: The attacker creates a GitHub issue with a visible request and hidden instructions in an HTML comment ... GitHub Actions workflows fire automatically on pull_request, issues, and issue_comment events, so simply opening a PR or filing an issue can trigger the AI agent without any action from the victim.

claim: Greptile is SOC2 Type II compliant, stores encrypted customer code until GitHub/GitLab access is revoked, and may use de-identified customer data for AI training unless the customer opts out; on-prem and bring-your-own-LLM options exist.
quote: Greptile may use de-identified customer data for AI training purposes ... If you do not wish to permit Greptile to engage in AI training, you may manage preferences and settings related to AI training within your account on the Platform.

claim: Three widely deployed AI coding agents were confirmed vulnerable to a single prompt-injection class with no external server needed; Anthropic rated its issue CVSS 9.4 Critical but paid only a $100 bounty.
quote: an attacker writes a malicious PR title or issue comment, the AI agent reads and processes it as trusted context, executes attacker-supplied instructions, and exfiltrates credentials back through a PR comment, issue comment, or git commit, no external server required.

claim: The CamoLeak attack hid prompts in PR descriptions and abused GitHub's Camo image proxy to exfiltrate AWS keys and private-repo data one character at a time; Legit Security's Omer Mayraz disclosed it and GitHub fixed it by disabling image rendering in Copilot Chat.
quote: hidden content that never appears when rendered by GitHub as HTML because it is ignored by the Markdown parser ... GitHub fixed it by disabling image rendering in Copilot Chat completely

claim: CamoLeak was tracked as CVE-2025-59145 with a CVSS score of 9.6, allowing silent theft of source code, API keys and secrets (including AWS keys and private zero-day descriptions) from private repositories via GitHub Copilot Chat.
quote: source code, API keys, and secrets from private repositories ... demonstration showed successful theft of AWS keys and privately stored zero-day vulnerability descriptions

claim: Effective April 24 2026, GitHub Copilot inputs, outputs and code snippets from Free/Pro/Pro+ tiers may be used for model training by default (opt-out), while Copilot Business and Enterprise are exempt.
quote: Copilot inputs, outputs, code snippets, and associated context may now be used for model training ... This is an opt-out policy. The setting defaults to enabled ... Covered (affected): Copilot Free, Pro, and Pro+ ... Exempt: Copilot Business, Copilot Enterprise

claim: Orca Security's RoguePilot (disclosed early 2026) exploited the integration between GitHub Issues and the in-Codespaces Copilot agent to achieve full repository takeover with no direct attacker interaction.
quote: RoguePilot

claim: Autonomous coding agents introduce supply-chain attack surface including tool/plugin poisoning, privilege escalation and cascading failures, with compromised agent plugins presenting as feature updates rather than malware.
quote: Autonomous agents introduce emerging risks, including prompt injection and manipulation, tool misuse and privilege escalation, memory poisoning, cascading failures, and supply chain attacks.

claim: Developer trust in AI accuracy fell from 40% to 29% in 2025 while favorability dropped from 72% to 60%, and 45% cite 'almost right, but not quite' AI output as their top frustration.
quote: trust in the accuracy of AI has fallen from 40% in previous years to just 29% this year. ... The number-one frustration, cited by 45% of respondents, is dealing with 'AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite.'

claim: Despite 84% of developers using AI tools, more actively distrust AI accuracy (46%) than trust it (33%), with only 3% saying they highly trust AI output, per the 2025 Stack Overflow survey.
quote: 84% of devs now use AI tools and 51% of pros use them daily, but trust hit an all-time low (46% distrust output, only 3% 'highly trust' it).

claim: The 2025 DORA report finds 30% of developers report little to no trust in AI-generated code, creating a 'verification tax' where time saved in creation is reallocated to auditing AI output.
quote: According to the 2025 DORA report, 30% of developers report little to no trust in AI-generated code. ... While I end up spending less time writing code, I spend more time babysitting the AI and reviewing what it is trying to do.

claim: Most AI code review platforms run 5-15% false positive rates, and teams progress from thorough investigation to 'dismiss all' within roughly 13 weeks as alert fatigue sets in.
quote: Most AI code review platforms operate between 5-15% false positive rates (FPR) ... Week 13+: 'I just click dismiss all now' ... 10% FPR translates to 2.5 wasted engineering hours per week

claim: Automation complacency research shows humans detect only ~30% of errors when AI is reliable versus ~75% when systems fail visibly, and developers with AI assistance wrote less secure code while believing it more secure.
quote: When AI is reliable, humans detect only ~30% of errors vs. ~75% when systems fail visibly (Parasuraman et al., 1993) ... Developers with AI assistance 'wrote significantly less secure code' yet 'were more likely to believe' it was secure (Perry et al., 2023)

claim: A 2025 systematic review of 35 peer-reviewed studies finds automation bias undermines competence by discouraging active reasoning and verification, weakening users' independent judgement and agency.
quote: automation bias—the tendency to over-rely on automated recommendations—has emerged as a critical challenge in human–AI collaboration ... it undermines competence by discouraging active reasoning and verification

claim: Microsoft researchers describe 'AI drag' where AI boosts seniors while undermining how juniors build expertise; a Harvard study of 62M workers found junior developer employment fell 9-10% within six quarters at AI-adopting firms while senior employment was unchanged.
quote: AI is making senior engineers dramatically more productive while simultaneously undermining the mechanisms through which junior engineers develop expertise ... Junior employment dropped 9-10% within six quarters at firms adopting AI ... Senior employment 'remained virtually unchanged'

claim: Code review's primary purpose is knowledge-sharing and education rather than bug-finding, a mentoring function AI tools bypass since they cannot grasp architectural intent or product trade-offs.
quote: treat every review as an opportunity for education and knowledge transfer, reframing code review as a primary mechanism for mentoring ... AI code review tools can surface hundreds of context signals, but they can't always understand architectural intent, product trade-offs

claim: AI coding assistant adoption reached 84% in 2026 while trust sits at only 29%, illustrating a widening adoption-trust gap.
quote: AI Coding Assistant Stats 2026: 84% Adoption, 29% Trust

claim: CodeRabbit Pro costs $24/seat/month annually or $30 monthly (a 25% premium), bills only developers who open PRs (a fluctuating, hard-to-budget count), and gates self-hosting behind custom-quoted Enterprise pricing.
quote: Only developers creating pull requests are charged, but this count can fluctuate month-to-month making budgeting unpredictable

claim: From June 1 2026 GitHub Copilot replaced premium request units with AI Credits (3,000/user/month dropping to 1,900 after Sept 1), and code review now consumes both AI Credits and GitHub Actions minutes as separate line items, with no cheaper-model fallback once credits run out.
quote: Once credits are gone, chat, agents, and code review stop entirely until the entitlement resets, or you buy more.

claim: Difficulty proving the ROI of AI-driven tools is a top organizational challenge, cited by 31% of Chief Sales Officers in a May 2026 Gartner survey.
quote: 31% of Chief Sales Officers Cited Difficulty Proving ROI of AI-driven Tools as a Top Challenge

claim: The 2025 DORA report frames AI value as a J-curve with a verification tax from reviewing AI-generated code, finds AI has a negative relationship with software-delivery stability absent strong controls, and reports 30% of developers have little or no trust in AI-generated code.
quote: AI adoption continues to have a negative relationship with software delivery stability

claim: Enterprise adoption of AI coding tools stalls because 79% of platforms lack publicly accessible SOC2 Type II attestation, forcing 90+ day vendor verification cycles while teams remain stuck evaluating questionnaires.
quote: 79% of platforms lack publicly accessible SOC2 Type II attestation, forcing compliance teams into 90+ day vendor verification cycles

claim: Fintech vendor security reviews typically take six to twelve weeks and probe data residency, subprocessor lists, breach notification, and whether customer data trains shared models, with most fintech compliance teams requiring opt-out or explicit opt-in for model training.
quote: These reviews typically take six to twelve weeks ... involve dozens of questions across security controls, data residency, subprocessor lists, breach notification timelines, and AI-specific concerns

claim: JFrog's 2026 supply-chain report finds an illusion of governance: 97% of organizations claim certified AI model governance yet 18% have no active governance over tools inside developer environments and only 57% govern MCP usage through automated controls, with governance needing to live at the pipeline level not the policy document.
quote: 18% of organizations have no active governance over the tools living inside their developers' environments.

claim: A 2026 governance gap exists where 98% of enterprises deploy agentic AI but 79% lack security policies, and a 2025 breach study found 63% of breached organizations lacked an AI governance policy at the time of the incident.
quote: 98% of enterprises deploy agentic AI, but 79% lack security policies

claim: Regulated sectors require AI code review tools with immutable audit trails for every review decision, PCI-DSS/SOC2 reporting, zero-code-retention, and HIPAA handling, since financial and healthcare data cannot leave the VPC without triggering GDPR, HIPAA, or SOC2 violations.
quote: when your AI agent processes customer financial data or patient health records, that data cannot leave your VPC without triggering GDPR, HIPAA, or SOC2 violations

claim: Enterprises in finance, government, defense, and healthcare often require AI code assistants deployable on-premises in air-gapped environments, with Tabnine (a 2025 Gartner Magic Quadrant Visionary) and Sourcegraph Cody (local Ollama inference of DeepSeek/Code Llama/Qwen models) cited as self-hosted options.
quote: often require solutions that can be deployed on-premises within secure, air-gapped environments isolated from the public internet

claim: The EU AI Act's August 2, 2026 enforcement date activates the main high-risk compliance framework (Articles 8-15), Article 50 transparency obligations for AI-generated content, and EU/national enforcement powers.
quote: The August 2, 2026 enforcement date activates the main high-risk AI compliance framework (including Articles 8-15, subject to certain exceptions), Article 50 transparency requirements for AI-generated content, and national and EU-level enforcement powers.

claim: AI-generated code is generally not copyrightable because U.S. copyright requires human authorship, leaving shippers with liability but no protection.
quote: The terms of service assign you ownership. The Copyright Office says there's nothing to own.

claim: The GitHub Copilot class action, filed in 2022 by the Joseph Saveri firm and Matthew Butterick, alleges Copilot reproduces open-source code while stripping copyright notices, license terms, and attribution.
quote: alleging that Copilot reproduces copyrighted open-source code while stripping copyright notices, license terms, and attribution

claim: Accountability practice holds that every AI recommendation needs a human reviewer accountable for the merge decision and no code should ship on automated approval alone.
quote: Every AI recommendation needs a human reviewer accountable for the decision to merge. No code should ship based solely on automated approval.

claim: Liability tends to follow the party best positioned to prevent harm, typically the organization integrating the AI system, even though responsibility appears distributed.
quote: the underlying legal principle is that liability follows the party best positioned to prevent harm. In an AI context, that tends to be the organization integrating the system into real-world decision-making.

claim: 2026 compliance expects human-readable AI audit trails capturing inputs, policies, retrieval sources, tool calls and approval states, with ISO/IEC 42001 emerging as the AI-governance management standard alongside SOC 2 and ISO 27001.
quote: Organizations need enough provenance to know what inputs, policies, retrieval sources, user requests, tool calls, and approval states shaped a decision.

claim: METR's 2025 RCT found 16 experienced open-source developers were 19% SLOWER with AI tools, while having forecast a 24% speedup beforehand and still believing afterward that AI sped them up by 20%.
quote: Developers expected AI to speed them up by 24% before the study. After experiencing the slowdown, they still believed AI had sped them up by 20%. 16 experienced developers participated... 246 total issues completed.

claim: In February 2026 METR redesigned its productivity experiment after finding selection bias (AI-optimistic developers refused to join no-AI conditions) and task cherry-picking, where 30-50% of developers avoided submitting tasks they thought AI would handle well, and called later subgroup speedup figures 'very weak evidence'.
quote: Between 30-50% of developers reported avoiding submission of tasks they believed AI could handle well... Later 2025 results showed speedups for some subgroups (-18% for returning developers, -4% for new ones), but researchers emphasize these figures are 'very weak evidence' due to selection effects.

claim: GitClear's 2025 analysis of 211M lines of code found code churn (revised within two weeks of commit) rose from 5.5% in 2020 to 7.9% in 2024, duplicated code blocks increased eightfold, and 2024 was the first year copy/pasted lines exceeded moved (refactored) lines.
quote: In 2024, 7.9% of all newly added code was revised within two weeks, compared to just 5.5% in 2020... the frequency of duplicated code blocks increased eightfold... 2024 was the first year when the number of copy/pasted lines exceeded the number of moved lines.

claim: The 2025 DORA report found AI now positively relates to delivery throughput (a reversal from 2024) but continues to have a NEGATIVE relationship with software delivery stability, and concludes AI amplifies existing team strengths and weaknesses rather than fixing them.
quote: AI adoption continues to have a negative relationship with software delivery stability... AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there. Strong teams use AI to become even better... Struggling teams will find that AI only highlights and intensifies their existing problems.

claim: Every AI code review vendor runs a self-favoring benchmark: Greptile claimed 82% recall on 50 PRs from 5 repos but scored only 45% when Augment Code re-evaluated the same repos; Qodo used LLM-generated synthetic bugs with unpublished ground truth, and competing vendors report incomparable F1 scores from 47.2% to 64% on different datasets.
quote: Each vendor runs their own benchmark, on their own dataset, and wins... Greptile: Reported '82% recall'... when Augment Code re-evaluated the same repos independently, Greptile's score dropped to 45%... F1 scores ranging from 47.2% to 64%, but each used different datasets, methodologies, and ground-truth construction approaches.

claim: The 'SWE-Bench Illusion' paper shows models identify buggy file paths with up to 76% accuracy using only issue text and no repository access (dropping to ~53% on outside-repo tasks), with 11.7-31.6% of instances showing verbatim memorization, concluding SWE-Bench scores reflect memorization not genuine problem-solving.
quote: State-of-the-art models achieved up to 76% accuracy identifying buggy file paths using only issue descriptions, without any repository structure or code access... 11.7% to 31.6% of test instances showed instance-level verbatim matching... reflects 'memorization rather than genuine problem-solving'.

claim: Independent audits of SWE-bench (SWE-Bench+) found 60.83% of successfully resolved issues involved solution leakage where the fix was provided or hinted in the issue text, and 47.93% of resolved issues passed only because of weak test cases.
quote: 60.83% of successfully resolved issues involve 'solution leakage', where solutions were either directly provided or indirectly hinted at in the issue report or comments... 47.93% of resolved issues were incorrectly marked as resolved due to patches passing weak test cases.

claim: LLM vulnerability detection F1 collapses on rare CWE categories: CWE-697 incorrect comparison 0.400, CWE-703 improper exception check 0.479, CWE-693 protection-mechanism failure 0.524, vs ~0.70 for common categories, with recall below 0.5 even for SOTA models.
quote: LLMs perform significantly worse on Rare vulnerabilities compared to Common ones ... Recall rates remain below 0.5 even for SOTA models, indicating systematic under-detection despite higher precision

claim: LLM vulnerability recall degrades sharply with multiple defects per file: Llama-3.3-70B drops from 94.4% (1 vuln) to 46.4% (9 vulns) in C, and Qwen2.5-32B perfect file-level accuracy on C++ collapses from 64.2% to 4.4%, giving incomplete reports 95% of the time on flawed files.
quote: in a real audit of a highly flawed file, this model would provide an incomplete report 95% of the time

claim: AI/static review catches structural bugs (race conditions, null pointers, resource leaks, pattern-based vulns like SQLi) but plateaus at ~50-60% security-vulnerability detection and systematically misses design flaws, missing authorization checks, and intent/requirements violations.
quote: the best static analysis tools plateaued at around 50-60% detection rates for security vulnerabilities ... a 2024 study found that 76% of warnings in vulnerable functions were irrelevant to the actual vulnerability

claim: Across 100 PRs with 580 injected issues (logic errors, edge cases, race conditions, resource leaks, error handling), most AI reviewers achieve high precision but extremely low recall, flagging only the most obvious problems and missing subtle, system-level, and cross-file issues; best tool F1 was 60.1%.
quote: recall is fundamentally constrained by the system's ability to deeply understand the codebase, cross-file dependencies, architectural context, and repository-specific standards

claim: On 118 self-contained runtime bugs across 45 repos, best AI reviewer detected only 48% (Macroscope, 98% precision), CodeRabbit 46%, and Greptile 24% (17/72), showing real-world per-bug catch rates well under half even before cross-service complexity.
quote: tested five tools against 118 self-contained runtime bugs across 45 open-source repositories, with Macroscope achieving the highest detection rate at 48% ... Greptile had a detection rate of 24%

claim: AI reviewers exhibit architectural blindness: they catch file-level issues but miss how changes affect dependent services and rarely detect breaking changes, a design-level limitation distinct from over-flagging style nitpicks that train reviewers to ignore the bot.
quote: Tools have architectural blindness: they catch file-level issues but miss how changes affect dependent services
